seo.title: IPC/WHMA-A-620 Wire Harness & Cable Assembly — Class 2 & 3
seo.description: Wire harness and cable assemblies built and inspected to IPC/WHMA-A-620 Class 2 and Class 3 in Brea, California. Prototypes from one piece, 100% continuity and hipot test, domestic build with no offshore subcontracting.

sections.title:
Every crimp inspected
to a *published standard*.
sections.text: IPC/WHMA-A-620 is the industry consensus standard for cable and wire harness assemblies — it defines exactly what an acceptable crimp, solder joint, splice, and shield termination looks like. Our operators and inspectors are certified to it, so “good enough” is never a judgement call made at a bench.

sections.heading: Class 1, 2, or 3 — and why it changes your price
sections.intro: This is the single most common source of quote-to-quote confusion in harness buying. Two shops can quote the same drawing and be 40% apart simply because they assumed different classes. Here's what each one actually means so you can specify it deliberately.
sections.caption: IPC/WHMA-A-620 product classes
rows: It needs to keep working, and downtime matters
It cannot fail, and it may be unrepairable in service
Industrial machinery, control panels, automotive, telecom
Aerospace, defense, medical, life support, space
sections.note: **Not sure?** Most industrial and control panel work is Class 2. If your harness goes into an aircraft, an implantable or life-supporting device, or a defense program, you are almost certainly Class 3 — and your customer's drawing usually says so. If it doesn't say, ask us before you buy on price.

sections.heading:
The harness shop is
down the hall
sections.text: Most panel builders buy harnesses from someone else, and most harness shops have never wired a panel. We do both in the same building — which means the harness is designed around the panel it goes into, and when something needs to change, it changes the same day instead of after a two-week vendor loop.

items.a: It means our operators and inspectors have been trained and certified against the standard, and that we build and inspect to its published acceptance criteria rather than to in-house opinion. The standard was developed by IPC and the Wire Harness Manufacturers Association and is the industry consensus document for cable and harness assemblies. Certification is maintained through recertification, not earned once.

items.q: I don't have a drawing. Can you still quote?
items.a: Usually. Send the harness you're replacing, or a wire list with connector part numbers and lengths, and we can work from that. For anything going into production we'll produce a controlled drawing so future lots are built identically — you own that drawing.

items.q: Do you have a minimum order quantity?
items.a: No. We build single prototypes, and we'd rather you validate one before ordering a thousand. Per-unit price does drop meaningfully at volume, and we'll show you the price break points in the quote.

items.q: Why is another quote so much cheaper?
items.a: Nine times out of ten it's one of three things: a lower IPC class assumed, a cheaper connector or wire substituted, or the work is being built offshore. None of those are automatically wrong — but they should be a decision you made, not a surprise you discovered. Our quotes state the class and the exact BOM so you can compare like for like.
Yes. 100% continuity test on every unit, with hipot where the application calls for it, and the test report ships with the lot. Crimps are pull-tested to the standard, and records are retained.
